subject: maths
prompt_en: For the perpendicular bisector of AB, Dev drew an arc of 5 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B, then joined the crossings. Check.
prompt_hi: AB ke perpendicular bisector ke liye Dev ne A se 5 cm aur B se 4 cm ka arc banaya, phir crossings ko joda. Check karo.
answer: Wrong: the radii must be equal; his crossing points are not equally far from A and B, so his line is not the perpendicular bisector

subject: maths
prompt_en: Compare bisecting an angle with a protractor and with a compass. Which method is exact in principle, and why?
prompt_hi: Protractor se aur compass se angle bisect karne ko compare karo. Kaunsa tareeka siddhant mein exact hai, aur kyun?
answer: The compass method: it depends on equal radii and congruent triangles, not on reading a scale, so it is exact for any angle

subject: maths
prompt_en: With only a compass and ruler, how can you cut a round roti into 4 equal pieces from the centre?
prompt_hi: Sirf compass aur ruler se ek gol roti ko centre se 4 barabar hisson mein kaise kaatoge?
answer: Draw a diameter through the centre, then construct its perpendicular bisector through the centre; the two lines make four 90° angles

subject: maths
prompt_en: Starting from 60° and bisecting, name three angles you can construct and say how.
prompt_hi: 60° aur bisecting se shuru karke, 3 angles batao jo bana sakte ho aur kaise.
answer: 30° (bisect 60°), 15° (bisect 30°), 120° (two 60°s side by side), 90° (60° + 30°) — any three

subject: maths
prompt_en: Teach a friend what makes a drawing a 'construction', using the perpendicular bisector as the example.
prompt_hi: Dost ko sikhao ki ek drawing 'construction' kab kehlati hai, perpendicular bisector ka example dekar.
answer: Only compass and straightedge; equal arcs (more than half AB) from A and B cross at two points equally far from both; joining them gives the perpendicular bisector, exact without measuring

subject: maths
prompt_en: From memory: which two tools are allowed in a construction?
prompt_hi: Yaad se: construction mein kaunse do tools allowed hain?
answer: A compass and an unmarked ruler (straightedge)

subject: maths
prompt_en: A regular pentagon's angle is 108°. Predict: will regular pentagons tile a floor? Then check with the angles.
prompt_hi: Regular pentagon ka angle 108° hai. Andaaza lagao: kya regular pentagons farsh tile karenge? Phir angles se check karo.
answer: No: 3 × 108° = 324°, leaving a 36° gap, and 4 would overlap (432°)

subject: maths
prompt_en: Why do equilateral triangles tile a floor but regular pentagons don't?
prompt_hi: Equilateral triangles farsh tile kyun karte hain par regular pentagons kyun nahi?
answer: 60° divides 360° exactly (6 triangles fit round a point), but 108° does not divide 360°

subject: maths
prompt_en: Om says regular octagons tile a floor on their own, because he has seen octagon tiles in a bathroom. Check.
prompt_hi: Om kehta hai regular octagons akele farsh tile kar dete hain, kyunki usne bathroom mein octagon tiles dekhe hain. Check karo.
answer: Wrong: 2 × 135° = 270° leaves a 90° gap; bathroom floors fill those gaps with small squares

subject: maths
prompt_en: Can any quadrilateral, even an odd-shaped one, tile a floor? Why?
prompt_hi: Kya koi bhi quadrilateral, chahe ajeeb shape ka ho, farsh tile kar sakta hai? Kyun?
answer: Yes: its four angles add to 360°, so four copies can meet at a point with each angle used once

subject: maths
prompt_en: Compare a scalene triangle and a regular pentagon. Which one tiles a floor, and why?
prompt_hi: Scalene triangle aur regular pentagon ko compare karo. Kaunsa farsh tile karta hai, aur kyun?
answer: The scalene triangle: 6 copies meet with each angle twice (2 × 180° = 360°); the pentagon leaves a 36° gap

subject: maths
prompt_en: A regular 12-sided polygon has angles of 150°. Can it tile a floor on its own? What gap would be left?
prompt_hi: Ek regular 12-sided polygon ke angle 150° hain. Kya yeh akela farsh tile kar sakta hai? Kitna gap bachega?
answer: No: 2 × 150° = 300°, leaving a 60° gap (which an equilateral triangle could fill)

subject: maths
prompt_en: Bees build their honeycomb with hexagon cells. Why are hexagons better than circles for this?
prompt_hi: Madhumakkhi honeycomb hexagon cells se banati hai. Iske liye hexagon circle se behtar kyun hain?
answer: Circles leave gaps between them; hexagons tile with no gaps and neighbouring cells share walls, saving wax

subject: maths
prompt_en: A floor uses regular octagons and small squares. At one corner, two octagons and one square meet. Show the angle sum.
prompt_hi: Ek farsh mein regular octagons aur chhote squares hain. Ek corner par do octagon aur ek square milte hain. Angles ka jod dikhao.

subject: maths
prompt_en: Teach a friend how to test whether a regular polygon can tile a floor on its own.
prompt_hi: Dost ko sikhao ki kaise check karein ki koi regular polygon akela farsh tile kar sakta hai ya nahi.
answer: Find its angle; if 360° divided by it is a whole number, copies fit round a point with no gap; only triangle, square and hexagon pass

subject: maths
prompt_en: From memory: which three regular polygons tile a floor on their own?
prompt_hi: Yaad se: kaunse 3 regular polygons akele farsh tile karte hain?
answer: Equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon

answer: Wrong: S = 6T; with 2 teachers there should be 12 students, but 6S = T would give a third of a student

subject: maths
prompt_en: Why is 'S = 6T' right and '6S = T' wrong for 6 times as many students as teachers?
prompt_hi: 6 guna students wali baat ke liye 'S = 6T' sahi aur '6S = T' galat kyun hai?
answer: Put T = 1: S = 6T gives 6 students, which fits; 6S = 1 gives S = 1/6, which does not

answer: n − 3: with n = 10 it gives 7, while 3 − n gives −7

prompt_en: Solve x ÷ 4 = 3 and 4x = 3. Why are the answers so different?
